text: I liked Dr. Chen, but the grading felt rough and uneven week to week. Still, the pacing kept me engaged despite my full-time job, and I barely missed any lectures—great for someone juggling study time, though feedback often came too late for real help.

OS had its ups and downs. with a full-time job, i barely had time to breathe, and the organization felt messy—deadlines drifting, notes scattered across forums and slides that didn’t always sync. dr. chen’s feedback was clear enough to trust my grade, but the few assessments mattered a lot, and the help from peers outpaced staff, especially during office hours where i asked about a memory management question and got a concrete pointer to the forum thread.

I’d say the course lands somewhere between “solid B, given I was juggling a full-time job” and “don’t rely on it if you want easy wins.” The lecturer was clearly capable and showed up with real-world chops, but the clarity sometimes felt rough—slides and explanations didn’t always line up, and I fell behind while trying to squeeze study time around deadlines. The software stack started rough at first and then settled into something workable, and office hours were a rescue when I got stuck on a debugging snag. Most work was solo, which fit my pace, though it did make the prerequisite feel heavier than advertised; I wouldn’t take it again, but it did push me enough to keep going.

I took Database Systems in my last semester because it fit my schedule more than my interests, and as a returning student I felt rusty but the basics came back enough to keep up. The platform and submission flow were smooth, but the examples felt thin and the move from accessible prerequisites to sharp ramp-up was jarring. I remember one late-night assignment that hinged on a tricky query plan, and it didn’t help that collaboration expectations were unclear.

I’m a returning student who felt a little rusty, and Cyber Security Basics fit the summer term with its compressed pacing, but the deadlines stacked up and I often felt rushed. I used the recorded lectures as needed; they’re useful but dry, and the early weeks start accessible yet ramp up sharply, so I spent more time on the short evening study blocks than I expected. The project on threat modeling helped, but feedback came sparse and late, so I wasn’t sure I was on the right track until it mattered.

Dr. Singh’s lectures in the Machine Learning course were clear and the pacing mostly kept on track, which helped given I needed it for a specialization. I started off engaged, but my attendance drifted mid‑semester as deadlines stacked up and the platform quirks caused extra stress; feedback often arrived too late to help fix things before the next task. The course works best if you’re in a study group, and I’ll remember that one week’s exam as a tough scramble more than the steady guidance.

I took Machine Learning as part of the required track because I’d heard it would be useful for industry work, and Prof. Alvarez is clearly capable, even if I’m new to the discipline and still learning the basics. The course is organized enough that I didn’t feel totally lost week to week, and the slides are serviceable for a quick recap, though they’re not particularly memorable, so I relied more on the problem sets to ground what we discussed. There aren’t many assessments, but each one feels weighty, which adds a constant edge of pressure—the kind where you want to get it right on the first try. The platform quirks sometimes create avoidable stress, like odd submission windows or scattered feedback notifications, which didn’t help my focus when I needed it most. I found the collaboration structure works best if you have a study group; alone, I felt adrift figuring out how to connect theory to the coding tasks. One concrete moment I still think about is the capstone-style project where a small error in feature scaling sent our model performance spiraling, a reminder that the basics matter a lot, even if the course tries to be fair. Would not take it again, even though it helped, judging it against my expectations rather than another course.

Midway through the semester, I’ve found Computer Networks surprisingly usable in practice, especially since the tooling and simulators I use at work line up with the concepts Dr. Chen covers. The course moves quickly enough that I wish the communication from the admin side was a bit clearer, but the support you actually get from fellow students is solid—people pipe up with quick explanations in the chat and share shortcuts for the labs. It starts approachable but ramps up fast, which feels like it mirrors a real industry leap from the easier prerequisite, and the assignments with frequent deadlines keep me on my toes. I’d take it again only if I already had a handle on time management, because I’d rather not juggle the chaos of deadlines, but I can’t deny it helped my day-to-day work a bit.

Last semester, I used the materials selectively, since the tooling felt neutral and messy at times; the lectures were uneven, deadlines stacked up unexpectedly, and collaboration expectations were unclear, but the content helped me link adjacent material, though I still failed.

I signed up for Data Structures out of genuine curiosity, hoping to finally get a solid sense of how these things actually fit together, but the summer term pacing felt suffocating in short evening sessions. The lectures from Dr. Miller were solid enough, and the LMS flow was smooth, which helped when I was juggling another hard class, but the overall difficulty was higher than I expected for a “foundations” vibe, especially since I was trying to fit it around late-night study blocks. Feedback timing was a mixed bag—some weeks the TAs pointed out concrete mistakes quickly, other weeks it felt like I had to chase hints; office hours ended up being the saving grace for me, a quick rescue when the code halted at the last minute.

I came into Computer Networks with genuine curiosity, but the early pace and the software stack felt rough enough to slow me down as I tried to fit study into short evening sessions. I appreciated that the prerequisite gaps cleared up more than I expected, and the instructor kept things clear enough that I could follow along, even as I was new to the discipline. The tooling got easier after a rocky start, though the platform still threw odd quirks that left me guessing at times, and the grading often seemed out of sync with what was talked about in lectures. Overall, I still remember the project and the late-night debugging session more than anything else, and that stuck with me.

the big gripe for me was the exam structure in the intro computer networks course this summer, where it felt like the questions assumed more prior exposure than the brochure suggested, so i walked into the first midterm already on edge about what the professor would consider fair to test. prof. haddad is clearly smart, and the lectures move quickly enough that i started out engaged, but attendance faded midsemester once the pacing felt compressed and the material kept looping back to tricky edge cases that didn’t get enough practice in the weekly labs. the LMS is actually smooth, submissions went through without drama, and i appreciated that aspect more than i expected, especially since deadlines tend to come in clusters and the auto-reminder system helped keep me from totally spacing. still, the instructions sometimes left too much interpretation, like a few questions on the project that could swing either way depending on which reading you focused on, which made the collaboration part feel hazy and the team dynamic a little uncertain. i’d say i’d only recommend taking it with a bit more preparation than the intro prerequisite implied, and maybe compare it to the easier prereq i took earlier, but don’t expect it to be a breeze. the whole thing left me tired and resigned, but i’ll admit the practical parts did teach me something about segmenting packets, even if the vibe was rough.

I’m new to this stuff, and the Database Systems intro felt heavier and less engaging than I’d hoped, especially with the chunky report-heavy weeks; the forums helped sometimes, but the vibe there could be a bit dismissive. Professor Rios’s grading rubric never felt clear, and juggling this plus another tough class made the week of the big memory-intensive exam feel rough.

I took Cyber Security Basics because I’m genuinely curious about how defenses actually work, and I was juggling a full-time job, which made the workload feel pretty real pretty fast. The project-heavy structure kept me engaged, but I left the midterm week frazzled and crunched, not sure I could have prepared any better given the time pressure. The forums helped when I ran into setup hiccups, though some threads felt a bit dismissive rather than constructive, which didn’t help a tired student mood. I’m glad the scores came quickly, but the explanations felt thin, almost like a checklist without much context for why certain choices mattered. I ended up in a C, and I’m not sure that result actually reflects my understanding, especially since the high-stakes exams and the big project both demanded different skills. There was one week—one memorable week—where the quiz and the lab felt tightly aligned, which I appreciated, but overall the tool setup and learning payoff didn’t quite feel proportional to the effort. Would I take it again? Probably not, even though it nudged me toward real questions I still think about.

Cyber Security Basics with Prof. Haddad felt like a mixed bag from someone who’s basically new to the field but trying to latch onto a few solid threads. The week-to-week patchiness in instruction left me uncertain about where the core ideas were landing, even as the recordings and notes kept me afloat during a busy term. Setting up the tooling was a pain at first, and I spent more time wrestling with the software stack than I’m comfortable admitting, though it did get smoother after a while. There was one memorable week on the exam format that still sticks with me—tight, high-stakes, and somehow fair. Office hours and TAs helped, but I wish the pacing and feedback felt more consistent.

Taking Computer Networks as my main focus this term, I did okay keeping up with nearly every lecture, even though the tooling sometimes sabotaged deadlines and made weeks feel extra tense. Dr. Chen is solid and the material builds on the prerequisites, but the admin side felt a bit murky—instructions left a lot of room for interpretation, which cost me time when I was juggling another hard class. The TAs were practical and responsive, which saved me during a couple of forum threads and quick office hours that week I was staring at a confusing router simulation. The standout memory is that midterm week, when one tricky lab question tied together the whole semester and I finally clicked; still, I wish the platform hadn’t hiccuped right before submission. Overall, it’s a tough, fair run, and I learned a lot, even if a few weeks felt rough.

I signed up for Database Systems as an advanced elective while juggling a full-time job, and I quickly realized I operate best when I can connect new stuff to what I already know, which helped a bit but also highlighted how much I’m rushing through things. Prof. Cohen moves through topics fast, and the explanations feel thin even when the grading rubric talks about depth; I walked away with a lot of questions that didn’t get fully answered, especially around how the data model decisions map to the practical work I do during the week. The course is mostly individual work, which didn’t help my tight weekly schedule, and the only time I felt any momentum was when a short, concrete example—like tweaking a query plan for a real-world dataset—made the whole thing click, even if it didn’t stick for long. I finished with a failed grade and mixed feelings, partly from the late, quick feedback that didn’t always map to what I struggled with, and partly from a stubborn sense that the material would make more sense if you’d already covered adjacent topics. It’s a tough fit if you’re already stretched thin, and I’m unlikely to take it again, despite the occasional value.

I signed up for Database Systems mostly out of genuine curiosity, but the experience was more of a slog than I expected. The course felt useful for understanding reasoning behind design choices, yet it wasn’t enjoyable, and I often felt like I was chasing a moving target. The project-heavy pace, with high-stakes exams, left me time-pressured most weeks, though I managed to catch up around deadlines. Feedback never came quickly enough—by the time I got a note, it was too late to adjust for the next task. Slides were serviceable but not memorable, and I think the material works best if you already know some adjacent topics; I struggled until I dropped into office hours and skimmed the TA forums for a clue.

Cyber Security Basics was a solid B for me, and I felt the effort matched the grade, especially since I came in with a strong coding background but weaker theory. The course builds on the prerequisites pretty cleanly, and by the midterm I could actually see how the pieces fit, even if the software stack was rough at first and then became manageable. I had to juggle full-time work, so I kept a loose schedule and a lot of the motivation dipped unpredictably, which made the project-heavy setup feel intense at times and almost casual at others. Prof. Rios was helpful when feedback finally came, but the messages felt sparse until it was almost too late to course-correct for the high-stakes exams. The best takeaway was finally getting a grip on the hands-on parts and the projects, though the pacing and the late-stage feedback were annoyances; I wish there had been more timely notes or check-ins. There were a couple of moments, like a late-night screencast showing how to wire the logging pipeline, that felt incidental but stuck with me. I’d only recommend it if you come prepared to push through the rough tooling and carve out time around work.

Calculus II felt unfair at the exam checkpoints, especially since I was balancing a full-time job and fell behind until deadlines nudged me back up. Prof. Haddad’s lectures are there, but the recorded ones can be dry, and the rapid pace with lots of assignments kept the pressure high; still, group work helped when we managed to function as a team. I’d probably not take it again, but it did push me to hustle and learn the core ideas anyway.

This was my last semester before graduation, and Linear Algebra felt like the kind of advanced elective that finally clicks after you’ve crammed a semester’s worth of notes into your brain. I mostly relied on recordings and notes, which saved me during busy weeks, but the lectures themselves were strong on big-picture ideas and the conceptual explanations that help “why this works” stuff stick, even if the example sets were a bit thin. The LMS and submission flow were smooth enough to not stress me out, which helped since I was juggling a few other courses and a looming thesis draft; the weirdly flexible deadline rhythm in the quizzes kept me thinking I had more time than I did, which was both nice and nerve-wracking. A single project on eigenbasis felt memorable in a low-key way, and the way it built on prerequisites made sense, but I still left with the sense that some concrete demonstrations were glossed over, like I kept asking for a tiny handhold that didn’t come. The collaboration expectations felt unclear—there were hints but no clear rules—which left me working solo more than I expected, even though the assessments were fair, they left me exhausted by the end of the term.

Linear Algebra clicked for me mostly because the recordings and notes fit a summer term with that compressed pace, and I could keep up without sprinting every night. The LMS flow was smooth, which helped when I procrastinated and binge-watched a few lectures before a deadline. I appreciated the feedback when it came through, though some weeks the notes felt vague and I wished for clearer guidance on how the curve was shaping our final grade. One week, the exam felt exhausting yet fair, like they tried to trap you with tricky wording but the logic still lined up if you’d done the practice. If you’re hopping in with adjacent math already in your back pocket, you’ll probably survive—maybe even enjoy the grind.

I took Operating Systems with Prof. Haddad as a mostly-recordings-and-notes person, and I’ll admit I liked him a lot more than I liked the grading. The lectures were clear enough when I watched them later, but the real lifeline for me was his office hours—the guy would actually walk through a failing concept with you, which saved the course more than once. The course feels best suited if you already know adjacent material; the prerequisite fit isn’t surface-level, it really helps to have some comfort with C or low-level concepts before you dive into the project-and-report heavy workload. The LMS and submission flow are smooth, which is nice when you’re juggling another hard class, but the assessment profile is time-consuming and the reports pile up fast. My one big annoyance is the curve-dependent grade; I ended up in an A after the curve, but the time spent polishing dense reports felt disproportionate to the final mark. A concrete habit I remember is the tight deadline pattern for weekly reports—one week you’re sprinting to wrap a design rationale, the next you’re chasing after a flaky test result. Overall, I’d still recommend him if you can lean on office hours, but be ready to invest real time into the paperwork.

I took Data Structures with Prof. Cohen mainly because it was a prerequisite for the specialization, and I did feel like I needed to prove I could handle mid-program core work, even though my motivation wobbled a bit week to week. The lectures were clear and the pacing was decent enough, but I noticed that the instructions for assignments sometimes left a lot to interpretation, which made deadlines stack up in ways I didn’t expect. The tooling felt approachable—the course materials and code examples were usable, and I appreciated that students helped each other out more than staff did when I hit a snag on the project scaffolding. I had enough time to study, but my motivation was inconsistent, and I found myself scrambling to keep up right before big milestones. There was a quick feedback loop—scores came back fast, though the explanations were thin, which left me unsure about where to fix things next. I wouldn’t take it again, even though I can see how the topics helped me, and I’d still generally recommend it to peers who need the prerequisite, but I’d brace for a few ambiguous prompts and a few late-evening cram sessions.

Cyber Security Basics with Dr. Park felt tough the whole term, and as a returning student I kept feeling rusty even though I showed up and did the bare minimum. The workload, especially around the weekly labs, was a grind—the tools and setup were frustrating and deadlines stretched by weeks of tooling hiccups made everything feel slower. I used the materials selectively, skipping a lot of the readings until I needed them, which left gaps when concepts clicked during the exams, like that one week where the mock scenario required a deeper dive than I expected. Communication via email support dragged during crunch times, and a few assignments had unclear collaboration expectations, which didn’t help when I was juggling other courses. The memorable week was the midterm with the tricky, short-answer section that reminded me how sharp I still need to be. Overall, not smooth, but there were moments that stuck.

I stuck with Machine Learning as my main focus that term, and I used the materials selectively when I needed them. Dr. Chen’s lectures are recorded and useful, but they feel dry and sometimes gloss over the practical connecting tissue, so I relied on peer discussions to actually decode the ideas. The pacing dragged during midterm crunch, and the grading rubric kept me guessing—some criteria felt vague, like where the emphasis actually landed for the final. Still, the prerequisite fit was solid, and I found the course worth it overall even though it wasn’t enjoyable in the moment, kind of useful without being fun. The one concrete thing I remember is juggling the project deadline around a heavy week, which didn’t help the vibe, but I’m glad I treated it as the main term course.

Taking Operating Systems with Dr. Chen was a must for my degree, so I leaned hard on it as my main focus that term. The grading felt fair after the curve, but the process was exhausting and the feedback varied a lot by assignment, which made it hard to know where I stood week to week. The setup for the tools and environments sucked up more time than it saved, and a lot of the platform quirks felt like a noise floor rather than learning signals. I appreciated the mix of exams and projects, even if the questions didn’t always map neatly to what was covered in lectures, and the policy communications were fine but occasionally sloppy, which added a layer of admin friction to the grind. Not sure I’d fully recommend, but I don’t regret the effort.

Back in the middle of a brutal mid-semester crunch, I signed up for Computer Networks hoping it would be a solid bridge to industry work, and I’ll admit the materials are solid—clear diagrams, good reference slides, and a few hands-on lab notes that actually helped me remember stuff I’d forgotten from last year. But the pacing is rough when deadlines stack up; the report-heavy cadence and the long writing workload felt relentless, especially with the weekly submissions piling on. Peer discussion saved me more than the official materials, and Prof. Rios actually seemed to lean into questions in those sessions, which helped me feel less rusty, even if the email support came through slowly when I needed quick feedback to hit a deadline. I don’t think I can fully recommend it, but there are pockets of value I won’t forget.

Taking Computer Networks during the summer with a full-time job, the project-heavy load and high-stakes quizzes made the pacing brutal, and the tooling setup was frustrating at first. I liked the instructor, but grading felt unclear and threw off my confidence.

I treated Data Structures as my main focus this term, a returner feeling a bit rusty and trying to push through the fundamentals again. The assessments felt clunky—the design didn’t click for me, with grading comments taking longer than I’d hoped and sometimes arriving after I’d moved on to the next topic. I used the platform and tools in fits and starts, doing the setup only when a deadline loomed, which made the payoff feel a bit askew. Collaboration felt murky; I wasn’t always sure what was expected, and email support during crunch weeks was slower than I’d like. Still, there were moments the material proved useful, and I’d broadly recommend others to try, even if it wasn’t enjoyable every week.

First semester, and I’m torn—the setup of the gear and the on-paper prerequisites are fine, but the few assignments hit hard and feel fair yet exhausting, especially since feedback drifts between quick notes and longer comments; I’m unsure whether the grade reflects my understanding, and I’d recommend only with solid prep.

I stuck with OS mostly via recordings after long work shifts, and the lectures were clear but the tooling glitches made deadline weeks feel pointless. I kept tanking the project on the mock scheduler, unsure if my grasp matched the grade, and the peer help felt louder than staff guidance.

i enrolled in the Machine Learning intro course hoping to bridge the gaps, and honestly the quick feedback helped me catch up right before deadlines. but the platform quirks were a headache and made pacing feel off, like a minor buzz I couldn't shake while trying to keep up with the proofs. the lectures were fine, but the tooling in practice was rough and the assessment mix didn’t always line up with what we covered in class. still, prof. rios kept things moving and the prerequisite gaps got filled better than i expected. at least one tiny project on a toy dataset stuck with me.

Dr. Park is clearly solid, easy to approach when I’m stuck, and the lectures are fine—slides are serviceable, not memorable, but they get the job done. I relied mostly on recordings and notes anyway, since the tool setup for the lab felt like more work than it paid off in learning, and I kept wishing the parsing scripts were a bit friendlier. Peer discussions sometimes sparked ideas that the official materials skimmed over, which helped when deadlines piled up on the assignment-heavy weeks. One concrete snag: the initial environment setup required three separate accounts and a weird path issue that ate a morning, which didn’t match how quickly I wanted to start coding. Compared to another course this term, this one felt more paced around quick-turno deadlines, but with less memorable watershed moments.

I stuck with almost every lecture, and at first I thought the lectures were clear and the pacing reasonable, but I kept tripping over the grading rubric that felt vague—like a map drawn in pencil that you’re supposed to follow but the landmarks don’t quite line up. The course builds on the basics, so prereqs fit, yet I remember misreading a problem on the first week and being tangled for a while, which shaped how I approached everything after. Office hours saved me more than once, turning a foggy debug into a concrete plan, even if the rest of the assessment still left me exhausted and chasing a moving target. By mid-term I wasn’t sure if I’d earned the curve, but I did manage an A after a curve, so the whole thing felt oddly mercurial. Overall, it’s a tough ride with some bright spots.

I took Data Structures in my first semester, chasing genuine curiosity, and the lectures were clear with decent pacing, though the quick feedback and thin explanations left me uncertain. Group work helped when the team clicked, and office hours at 5 pm after a long test discussion stick in my memory.

I learned practical stuff in Computer Networks, but the platform quirks and late feedback made it stressy; still, Dr. Chen’s office hours saved me when I struggled with the early routing confusion, and I’d still recommend it.

Calculus II with Prof. Cohen was fair on the big exam, which I appreciated given I juggle a full-time job. I kept up with nearly every lecture, and the pacing was okay, but the platform quirks gave me some avoidable stress, especially during problem set submissions. The forums helped, though sometimes they veered a bit dismissive; a study group made the material click for me, and I’d still recommend it to others who can flex around the quirks.

I’m a returning student who felt a bit rusty walking into Dr. Park’s Operating Systems course, and I appreciated how the lectures stayed approachable even as the material started to ramp up fast. The early weeks clicked well enough, thanks to the clear explanations, but I’ll admit the platform quirks and the heavy, report-style workload kept a steady drumbeat of stress—especially when deadlines stacked on a single day. I liked how the feedback was thorough and constructive, and I could see the logic in the grading approach, even when the heavy reports ate into time I’d hoped to spend on other demanding courses. One memory that sticks is the moment I misinterpreted a memory-management concept and spent a night revisiting page tables, which oddly shaped how I approached every subsequent assignment. The email support, though, felt slow right when deadlines loomed large, so I relied more on peer notes—which wasn’t ideal for a course that’s supposed to be introductory and accessible. Overall I’d still recommend it broadly, especially if you keep your wits about the pacing and lean on the early momentum rather than the late surge.

I’m in my last semester and tried to fit Linear Algebra into short evening study bursts, which makes the pacing feel rough even though the material isn’t impossible. Prof. Cohen’s recorded lectures are useful but a bit dry, and explanations after the quick quizzes feel skimmed; still, the prereqs click into place better than I expected. The group help seems to come from us more than from staff, and the assessment felt fair but exhausting, like the workload never quite lets up.

When I started Data Structures, I was totally new to the discipline and the basics, and it felt approachable at first but then the pace really ramps up, which made me nervous about keeping up since the prerequisite fits: it starts accessible but quickly gets sharper. Prof. Alvarez lectures were worth a listen, and the recorded videos helped when I fell behind, though they were a bit dry, so I often needed a quick burn with the slides to stay awake. The course seems to run best if you have a study group, because I found the collaboration structure weak on its own—late comments on assignments like the linked list exercise would’ve helped if I could compare notes with someone else before the deadline. Grading comments are detailed and I did appreciate the explicit notes on where my complexity analysis went wrong, but the feedback came a bit delayed, which made it hard to adjust for the next assignment. I remember one office-hours visit where the TA walked me through a concrete bug in my hash table implementation, which saved me hours, and that memory anchors my view: useful, but not exactly enjoyable. Overall, it’s useful for the degree, even if the vibe is mostly work and not fun.

So I picked Cyber Security Basics because it’s required for the degree, and I tried to make it my main focus this term. The pacing felt rough at times—it starts accessible but then ramps up quickly, and I’m new to the discipline, so I spent a lot of evenings second-guessing whether I should push through or ask for help. Group work helped when the team actually functioned, but feedback quality varied by assignment and the timelines annoyingly inconsistent.

Linear Algebra with Dr. Singh felt doable but only if I used the material selectively, especially since the lectures are dry to slog through, even when the recordings are clear. The grading is transparent enough, and the curve helped me land in the A band after a timely bounce-back on a couple of tough assignments, but I kept juggling short evening study blocks around the frequent deadlines. Office hours were a lifeline—one quick visit helped me untangle a stubborn matrix problem, and the feedback came back fast enough to adjust my approach for the next deadline. I compared it to the prerequisite, which was smoother, and I’ll admit I relied on the practice sets more than the live sessions, but I still appreciated how the course kept me moving rather than letting me drift.

I’m a returning student who felt rusty, and Machine Learning felt accessible at first but ramped up fast and left me behind. The LMS and submission flow were smooth, but the tooling setup was a headache—VMs wouldn’t deploy, and I spent a ridiculous amount of time chasing environment issues during a mid-semester crunch. The project-heavy format and high-stakes exams didn’t help me recover my footing; I’d still skip it if I could, though I did pick up a few practical tricks I’ll probably forget faster than I’d like.

I’m glad I pushed through Cyber Security Basics, but the materials felt thin for someone with a coding-heavy background and weaker theory. The lectures were solid, but the handouts and reading felt rushed and didn’t connect the concepts to real-world setups I care about, which left me hunting for extra sources. Grading updates came fast, but the explanations were sketchy, and feedback often arrived too late to adjust my approach for the next task. Group work helped when teammates were on the same page, and the LMS submission flow is smooth enough to not fight you, which was a small relief. I’d only recommend it if you’re prepared to fill gaps on your own and stick with the instructor through office hours; I remember a useful office-hours chat about attack surfaces that kept me going.

Machine Learning in the first semester was a solid fit for my evenings, since I could squeeze in short sessions after dinner and still feel like I was making real progress. I appreciated the relevance and the materials, which were approachable for someone who’s comfy with proofs but not much into systems, and I could actually see how the theory would map to something you could try in a notebook or on a small dataset. The group work sometimes clicked—when the team functioned well we could split the heavy lifting and I felt like the practical ideas started sticking. Still, the tooling setup and the admin side were a constant headache, with conflicting instructions and a few quirky dependencies that dragged on the first couple weeks. The assessment felt very heavy on reports and it took ages to get through the rubric, which made the workload feel more time-consuming than it should have been for an advanced elective. Our instructor’s delivery was a bit uneven week to week, and I found myself relying on the lecture notes more than I’d like, though the core concepts and the emphasis on practical application kept the course moving forward. Overall, I’d compare it to another course from the term and recognize the value, even if I wouldn’t take this exact track again.

I started Cyber Security Basics with genuine curiosity, but I ended up feeling mixed after the mid‑semester crunch and a few vague grading moments. The peer discussions saved some effort, and the course filled gaps I didn’t realize I had, though the grading rubric felt fuzzy and late email support didn’t help when deadlines piled up. Still, I liked the instructor, and the one incident with the week-before-project push sticks with me.

Starting Linear Algebra with Dr. Park was rough: I was juggling a full-time job, attendance faded mid-semester, and the materials were not helping my basic grasp, though class organization kept things on track; feedback arrives late, exams were exhausting but fair. One memorable week was the final project crunch.

I took Cyber Security Basics because I heard it would be useful for industry work, and there were moments where it clicked, even if I fell behind at times and then tried to sprint to catch up around deadlines. The course starts accessible but ramps up sharply, which made the early weeks feel manageable and the later ones oddly generous with the workload and tighter on the grading timing. I appreciated that the material is approachable, but the grading rubric always felt vague in its expectations, so I wasn’t sure what exactly would move the needle on a final grade, especially since the curve finally boosted me to an A. The tooling and platform threw a wrench during deadline weeks, with some quiet crashes and weird submission hiccups that made a couple of assignments feel luck-based rather than earned. I found the course works best if you have a study group, since collaborating helped parse the tougher concepts and kept motivation from wandering. There’s a memorable week around the practical security assessment that stuck with me, even though I wouldn’t take this course again. Overall, mixed vibes, mixed pacing, but it did land some useful takeaways.

Took Computer Networks with Prof. Rios mid-program, and I barely passed after grinding through most of the term. The project-heavy setup and high-stakes exams forced me to make the course my main focus that term, and the quick feedback helped me adjust, but the tooling setup was a nightmare until late in the term. The slides are serviceable but not memorable, and I wish the forums or TAs were more proactive with quick clarifications.
